titre: The Vampyre of 1819 Appeared Under Byron's Name
accroche: On April 1, 1819, a London magazine publishes The Vampyre “by Lord Byron.” Its real author, Polidori, has to write in to be recognized.
contenu_vulgarise:
Ask who wrote the first great vampire story in English: people often think of Bram Stoker, in 1897. Seventy-eight years earlier, a much shorter text had already fixed the character. And it first appeared under someone else's signature.

## A Story Signed With the Wrong Name

On April 1, 1819, *The New Monthly Magazine*, in London, publishes in its issue no. 63 a story titled “The Vampyre; a Tale by Lord Byron.” It is preceded by an “extract of a letter from Geneva” that evokes the summer of 1816, near Lake Geneva, when Lord Byron and his companions told one another ghost stories, and that presents the story as drawn from an outline by Byron. That same season of 1816 saw the birth of Mary Shelley's *Frankenstein*, in the same circle.

But Byron did not write *The Vampyre*. The author is John William Polidori, who had accompanied him to Switzerland as physician and secretary. Byron had begun a fragment of a story; Polidori made the tale out of it.

## The Correction the Following Month

In issue no. 64, Polidori writes to the editor. He presents himself as the person targeted by the letter from Geneva and corrects it: the correspondent is mistaken in attributing the tale, in its present form, to Byron. The starting point is Byron's, the development is his own, written at the request of a lady who judged that nothing could be made of what Byron had planned.

The correction was not enough. The story appears in book form the same year from Sherwood, Neely and Jones, with Byron's name on the title page. After Polidori's protest, later printings remove that name without putting his own in its place. Byron and Polidori both denied it repeatedly, and the attribution long circulated in spite of them.

## Why It Was Believed

The villain of the story is called Lord Ruthven. That name had already been used in *Glenarvon*, the novel by Lady Caroline Lamb published in 1816, in which a thinly disguised Byron character is named Clarence de Ruthven. A reader of 1819 could therefore recognize a portrait of Byron in it, and some critics wonder whether Polidori was settling a score with him there.

## What the Story Fixed

Before Polidori, the vampire is a creature of folklore. In his hands, it is an aristocrat who moves in good society and makes his victims there. This model carried through the 19th century, and the themes of the tale continued to influence *Dracula*, in 1897.

It remains to be seen what the first readers believed they were reading: a tale by Byron, or a portrait of Byron as a vampire lord.

quiz.question: What does Polidori's letter, published in the next issue of the magazine, reveal?
choix: That Byron dictated the story to him and ceded him the rights
That he wrote the story in London, without having known Byron in 1816
That he himself developed an outline by Byron, so the tale is not entirely his
That the story is the translation of a German tale read at the Villa Diodati
quiz.explication: Polidori writes that the starting point is indeed Byron's but the development is his own, at the request of a lady. He did not write alone in London: he was traveling with Byron as physician and secretary. No transfer of rights or German translation is mentioned.

quiz_supplementaire.question: After Polidori's protest, how does the book edition correct the attribution in its later printings?
choix: It adds Polidori's name next to Byron's
It removes Byron's name without putting Polidori's in its place
It republishes the text under an anonymous author named “a gentleman”
It withdraws the story from all later editions
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Later printings remove Byron's name from the title page, but without putting Polidori's in its place: the attribution remains uncertain despite the denials of both men.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Where does the name of the character Lord Ruthven, the vampire of the story, come from?
choix: From a Scottish friend of Polidori's who died during the trip to Switzerland
From a real marquis whom Polidori had treated in Geneva
From a character invented by Byron himself in his fragment
From a character in Glenarvon, Lady Caroline Lamb's novel published in 1816
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Lord Ruthven takes the name of Clarence de Ruthven, a character inspired by Byron in Glenarvon, Lady Caroline Lamb's novel published in 1816, by the same publisher.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Polidori's vampire differ from the folklore creature that precedes it?
choix: He is an aristocrat who moves in good society and chooses his victims there
He is an isolated peasant who never leaves his village
He is an invisible creature with no human appearance
He is a comic character who parodies Gothic tales
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Before Polidori, the vampire is a creature of folklore; in his hands, it becomes an aristocrat who moves in good society and makes his victims there, a model that runs through the whole 19th century.
